title: Surgical intervention ≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours after injury for the management of acute traumatic central cord syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
condition_or_topic: Acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS) and the timing of surgical intervention
clinical_background: ATCCS accounts for a substantial share of spinal cord injuries and typically involves greater weakness in the upper limbs than in the lower limbs, with sensory loss and bladder dysfunction. It often follows a hyperextension injury in someone with underlying cervical spondylosis or stenosis. The optimal timing of surgery remains disputed: some clinical studies suggest that intervention within 24 hours may improve neurological outcomes and shorten hospital stays, whereas arguments for surgery after 24 hours emphasize time for medical optimization and a possible reduction in perioperative risks and mortality.
objectives: Evaluate how surgery performed ≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours after injury affects efficacy, patient outcomes, and complications in ATCCS.
Integrate findings from studies worldwide to quantify the effect of surgical timing on prognosis in ATCCS.
clinical_question: In patients with ATCCS, how does surgery ≤ 24 hours after injury, compared with surgery > 24 hours after injury, affect functional outcomes and complications?
interpretation: Surgery performed ≤ 24 hours after injury was associated with fewer surgical complications than surgery performed > 24 hours after injury (1.2% vs 4.5%, p = 0.05). The earlier group had greater improvement in ASIA motor score at a weighted mean follow-up of 12 months, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant (mean difference 12, 95% CI −20.7 to 44.6, p = 0.33). The authors regard the complication finding as a possible safety advantage of earlier surgery, not as a reason to disregard differences between patients and injuries. They speculate that shorter spinal cord compression or a shorter preoperative stay might contribute to the finding, but do not establish its cause.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The lower complication rate with earlier surgery contrasts with the perception that early intervention carries greater surgical risk. A meta-analysis by Liu et al. also found fewer complications with early decompression for traumatic spinal cord injury (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.91, p = 0.02) and a shorter hospital stay (mean day difference −4.76 days, 95% CI −9.19 to −0.32, p = 0.04); the present study lacked sufficient data to assess length of stay. In a prospective cohort reported by Fehlings et al., complications were more frequent after late than early surgery (30.5% vs 24.2%), although that difference was not statistically significant. Unlike the present analysis, Liu et al. reported a significant association between early surgery and better neurological outcomes (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.19–2.31, p < 0.01). Fehlings et al. likewise reported greater odds of improvement with early surgery at 6-month follow-up (OR 2.83, 95% CI 1.10–7.28, p = 0.03). The authors attribute the difference between their neurological finding and the broader spinal cord injury literature primarily to their specific focus on ATCCS and the defined surgical time frames.
clinical_implications: Intervention ≤ 24 hours may offer a safety benefit for patients with ATCCS, but the authors advise cautious interpretation of the complication finding.
The analysis did not establish a statistically significant neurological advantage for surgery ≤ 24 hours rather than > 24 hours.
practice_implications: Surgical decisions should be individualized according to each patient's clinical characteristics and injury pattern, despite the observed trend favoring earlier intervention.
limitations: All included articles provided level IV evidence, and differences in study quality and publication heterogeneity could affect the findings.
Surgical complications were uncommon despite the statistically significant difference between groups.

Most included articles did not report comorbidities, limiting assessment of their role in delayed surgery; a greater burden of comorbidities in the > 24-hour group could have confounded the comparison.
Missing or inconsistently reported information could have affected the analyses.
Variation in patient populations, surgical techniques, and outcome measures could limit comparability across studies.
The available data were insufficient to analyze length of hospital stay.
strengths: The authors state that the groups had comparable neurological status at admission, lending greater reliability to the comparison.
The specific focus on ATCCS and the defined intervention time frames allowed a more nuanced examination of early surgery in this population.
open_questions: Whether surgery ≤ 24 hours improves neurological recovery in ATCCS remains unresolved.
The reasons for the observed difference in complication rates remain uncertain.
future_directions: Further research is needed to confirm the findings and clarify their clinical implications.
The proposed explanations for the lower complication rate with earlier surgery warrant further investigation.
study_design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of retrospective and prospective studies comparing surgery ≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours after injury in patients with ATCCS. The review followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane were searched from database inception through September 2022. Two authors independently screened records and full texts, with disagreements resolved by a third author; extracted data were independently verified.

population.description: Patients with ATCCS who underwent surgery: 188 (38.5%) in the ≤ 24-hour group and 300 (61.5%) in the > 24-hour group.
inclusion_criteria: Retrospective or prospective research involving patients with ATCCS.
Reporting of clinical characteristics, treatment approach, and outcomes.
exclusion_criteria: Meta-analyses, reviews, editorials, letters, books, or book chapters.
Insufficient clinical detail on patient demographics, treatment methods, and/or outcomes.
population.mean_age: Weighted mean age: 52.4 years (95% CI 44.9–61.2 years) in the ≤ 24-hour group and 55.2 years (95% CI 49.3–61.8 years) in the > 24-hour group.

interventions: Surgery ≤ 24 hours after injury for ATCCS.
comparators: Surgery > 24 hours after injury for ATCCS.

primary: Clinical characteristics of surgically treated patients with ATCCS.
Functional outcomes, including change in ASIA motor score at the last follow-up.

statistical_methods: Analyses used R version 4.1.1, RStudio version 2021.09.0, and the meta package in R. Categorical data were summarized as frequencies with percentages or weighted frequencies with 95% CI; continuous data were summarized as weighted means with 95% CI or medians with interquartile ranges. Differences in medians were assessed with the Mann-Whitney U-test. Proportional meta-analysis pooled aggregate proportions after logit transformation, while meta-analysis of means pooled means. Subgroup analyses assessed between-group differences, and mean differences quantified changes in ASIA motor score at the last follow-up. All studies were combined with random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using the chi-square test and Higgins I2 test. Two-tailed p values less than 0.1 were considered statistically significant. Publication bias was examined visually with funnel plots; although Egger’s test was planned with p values < 0.05 indicating bias, no endpoint had enough articles (n ≥ 9) for that test.
follow_up: Median clinical follow-up was 12 months (IQR 3–36) in both groups.
quality_assessment_tool: 2011 Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine guidelines

main_findings.description: Surgical complications were significantly more frequent after surgery performed > 24 hours after injury than after surgery performed ≤ 24 hours after injury.
main_findings.context: The analysis used patients with available surgical-complication data.

main_findings.description: Improvement in ASIA motor score was greater in the ≤ 24-hour group, but the between-group difference was not statistically significant.
main_findings.metric: mean difference in ASIA motor score improvement
main_findings.context: The comparison favored the ≤ 24-hour group over the > 24-hour group at a mean of 12 months after surgery. Study data were combined using random-effects models; an I² value and prediction interval for this outcome were not reported.

main_findings.description: The groups did not differ significantly in ASIA motor score at admission.
main_findings.context: Admission neurological status was assessed before the compared surgical interventions.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Surgical complications occurred in 2/172 (1.2) patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 12/266 (4.5) patients in the > 24-hour group (p = 0.05).

secondary_results: The search identified 1800 articles; 1326 remained after duplicate removal, 1292 were excluded following title and abstract assessment, and 27 of the 34 assessed in full were excluded. The review included 7 articles, all classified as level IV evidence, covering 488 patients: 188 (38.5%) underwent surgery ≤ 24 hours after injury and 300 (61.5%) underwent surgery > 24 hours after injury.

Among patients with sex data, males accounted for 127/172 (73.8) in the ≤ 24-hour group and 212/266 (79.7) in the > 24-hour group (p = 0.15). Weighted mean age was 52.4 years (95% CI 44.9–61.2 years) and 55.2 years (95% CI 49.3–61.8 years), respectively (p = 0.47).

Mechanism-of-injury data were available for 165 patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 236 in the > 24-hour group. Falls accounted for 81 (49.1) versus 142 (60.2) (p = 0.32); motor vehicle accidents, 54 (32.7) versus 67 (28.4) (p = 0.31); sports-related trauma, 6 (3.6) versus 4 (1.7) (p = 0.22); and other mechanisms, 24 (14.5) versus 23 (9.7) (p = 0.42). The Results text reports no overall difference in injury mechanism (p = 0.32), whereas the Discussion gives p = 0.11 for comparable mechanism frequencies.

Spinal cord compression-level data were available for 130 patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 152 in the > 24-hour group. C3–4 compression occurred in 17 (13.1) versus 25 (16.4) (p = 0.50); C4–5 compression in 102 (78.5) versus 108 (71.1) (p = 0.73); and compression at other levels in 11 (8.5) versus 19 (12.5) (p = 0.55). The reported overall comparison was not significant (p = 0.35).

Neuroimaging data were available for 89 patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 207 in the > 24-hour group. Cervical stenosis was reported in 65 (73) versus 139 (67.1) (p = 0.31); disc herniation/fracture/dislocation in 16 (18) versus 41 (19.8) (p = 0.53); and cord edema in 8 (9) versus 27 (13) (p = 0.37). The Results text also describes the between-group neuroimaging findings as nonsignificant with p > 0.53, which does not agree with the individual p values in the table.
Steroids were administered to 69/129 (53.5) patients with available data in the ≤ 24-hour group and 65/152 (42.8) in the > 24-hour group; the difference was not significant (p = 0.72).

Surgical-approach data were available for 49 patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 136 in the > 24-hour group. An anterior approach was used in 22 (44.9) versus 51 (37.5), a posterior approach in 17 (34.7) versus 68 (50), and a combined approach in 10 (20.4) versus 17 (12.5). The overall approach comparison was not significant (p = 0.14).
Median clinical follow-up was 12 months (IQR 3–36) in both surgical-timing groups (p > 0.99).

In a cited meta-analysis by Liu et al. concerning traumatic spinal cord injury, the late (≥ 24 hours) group had a significantly higher complication rate (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.91, p = 0.02). That analysis also associated surgery within 24 hours with a shorter hospital stay (mean day difference −4.76 days, 95% CI −9.19 to −0.32, p = 0.04) and better neurological outcomes (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.19–2.31, p < 0.01). Length of stay could not be analyzed in the present review because its available data were insufficient.

In a cited prospective cohort study by Fehlings et al. of acute spinal cord injury, complications occurred in 30.5% of the late (≥ 24 hours) group and 24.2% of the early (< 24 hours) group; that difference was not statistically significant. At 6-month follow-up, early-surgery patients were 2.8 times more likely to improve by at least 2 grades in the ASIA motor score after adjustment for preoperative neurological status and steroid use (OR 2.83, 95% CI 1.10–7.28, p = 0.03).

Another cited study of traumatic spinal cord injury reported improvement of at least 2 grades on the ASIA scale in 27.2% of patients treated within 24 hours, compared with 3% treated later (p = 0.01).

For injury-mechanism context, the cited study by Rodríguez-Meza et al. attributed spinal cord injury to falls in 41.6% of patients. A separate cited international epidemiological study attributed 25% to 67% of spinal cord injuries to motor vehicle accidents and 5% to 28% to contact sports.

main_conclusion: For patients with ATCCS, surgery within ≤ 24 hours was associated with a significantly lower surgical complication rate than surgery after > 24 hours, but neurological outcomes did not differ significantly. The authors advise tailoring surgical decisions to each patient’s clinical features and injury pattern.
narrative_summary:
This systematic review and meta-analysis compared surgery within ≤ 24 hours of injury with surgery after > 24 hours for acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS). It included 7 articles and 488 patients: 188 (38.5%) underwent earlier surgery and 300 (61.5%) underwent later surgery. The included articles provided level IV evidence. The groups were broadly similar in demographic characteristics, injury findings, neurological status at admission, steroid administration and surgical approach.

Among patients with complication data, surgical complications occurred in 2/172 (1.2) in the ≤ 24-hour group and 12/266 (4.5) in the > 24-hour group (p = 0.05). Median clinical follow-up was 12 months (IQR 3–36) in both groups (p > 0.99). At a mean of 12 months, improvement in ASIA motor score was greater with earlier surgery, but the between-group mean difference of 12 (95% CI −20.7 to 44.6, p = 0.33) was not statistically significant.

The authors interpret the lower complication rate as a potential safety advantage of earlier intervention, not as evidence of superior neurological recovery. They caution that all included studies offered level IV evidence, complications were uncommon, and incomplete comorbidity reporting and variation between studies could affect interpretation. They recommend individualized decisions based on clinical characteristics and injury patterns.

document_sections.heading: OBJECTIVE
document_sections.content: The authors sought to compare the effectiveness, outcomes, and complications of surgery performed ≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours after injury in patients with acute traumatic central cord syndrome (ATCCS).

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The authors searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane and conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of treatment and outcomes. The abstract identifies the reporting guidelines as Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRIMSA).

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: The review included 7 articles and 488 patients: 188 (38.5%) underwent surgery ≤ 24 hours after injury, and 300 (61.5%) underwent surgery > 24 hours after injury. The groups did not differ significantly in demographics, injury mechanism, spinal cord compression level, neuroimaging findings, or admission American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) motor score. Surgical approach and steroid use were similar. Surgical complications were significantly more frequent in the > 24-hour group (4.5%) than in the ≤ 24-hour group (1.2%) (p = 0.05). Clinical follow-up was 12 months (interquartile range 3–36) in both groups (p > 0.99). Improvement in ASIA motor score favored the ≤ 24-hour group but was not statistically significant; the mean difference was 12 (95% CI −20.7 to 44.6).

document_sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
document_sections.content: Surgery ≤ 24 hours after injury may offer an advantage for patients with ATCCS through fewer complications. The authors state that more research is required to establish whether this finding and its clinical implications are confirmed.

document_sections.heading: Surgical intervention ≤ 24 hours versus > 24 hours after injury for the management of acute traumatic central cord syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
document_sections.content: ATCCS accounts for a substantial share of spinal cord injuries and poses a management challenge. Upper-limb weakness is greater than lower-limb weakness; sensory impairment and bladder dysfunction can also occur. Hyperextension injury in a patient with underlying cervical spondylosis or stenosis is a frequent cause. The best timing for surgery remains disputed. Some clinical studies suggest that intervention within 24 hours may improve neurological outcomes and shorten hospitalization. Other studies favor surgery beyond 24 hours because the delay may permit medical optimization and potentially lower perioperative risk and mortality. Given the conflicting evidence, the authors undertook a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing surgery ≤ 24 hours with surgery > 24 hours in ATCCS. They aimed to quantify how timing relates to prognosis across studies and to inform clinical decisions and evidence-based guidance.

document_sections.heading: Literature Search
document_sections.content: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis under the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. They searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane from database inception through September 2022. Searches combined Medical Subject Headings and keywords with Boolean operators, including (Central Cord Syndrome) AND (Surgery OR Surgical OR Management OR Treatment OR Intervention).

document_sections.heading: Study Selection
document_sections.content: Prespecified eligibility criteria admitted retrospective or prospective studies of patients with ATCCS that supplied clinical characteristics, treatment information, and outcomes. The authors excluded meta-analyses, reviews, editorials, letters, books, and book chapters; reports with fewer than 5 cases; studies lacking sufficient demographic, treatment, and/or outcome details; and publications not written in English. J.Q. and K.B. independently screened titles and abstracts and then assessed eligible full texts. O.B.A. resolved disagreements. The authors also examined reference lists for additional studies.

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction
document_sections.content: J.Q. extracted study data, which O.B.A. independently checked. Recorded variables were authorship, publication year, study design, sample size, patient age and sex, injury type and mechanism, injury level, ASIA motor scores at presentation and final follow-up, management, and complications. Information could be absent because an original study did not report it or did not present it separately.

document_sections.heading: Data Synthesis
document_sections.content: The main outcomes concerned clinical characteristics, operative treatment, and functional results among surgically treated patients with ATCCS. The authors evaluated each article's evidence quality using the 2011 Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine guidelines.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Analyses used R version 4.1.1 and RStudio version 2021.09.0; the meta package supported meta-analyses, heterogeneity and publication-bias assessments, and subgroup analyses. Categorical results were expressed as frequencies with percentages or weighted frequencies with 95% CI. Continuous results were expressed as weighted means with 95% CI or medians with interquartile range (IQR); median differences were assessed with the Mann-Whitney U-test. Proportional meta-analysis pooled aggregate proportions, while a meta-analysis of means pooled means. Subgroup analyses assessed between-group differences. Because included studies used the same scoring system, the authors calculated mean differences in ASIA motor score change at final follow-up. Proportions underwent logit transformation before pooling to limit skew and overstated precision. The significance criterion was p values less than 0.1 for 2-tailed tests. All studies were pooled with random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed with the chi-square test and Higgins I2 test. Funnel plots were used to examine publication bias; Egger’s test would have treated p values < 0.05 as evidence of bias. Visual symmetry was inspected for all studies. No endpoint had enough articles (n ≥ 9) for Egger’s test.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The database searches identified 1800 candidate articles. Removing duplicates left 1326 unique articles. Title and abstract screening excluded 1292, leaving 34 for full-text assessment. Full-text review excluded 27 that failed eligibility criteria. The final synthesis contained 7 articles with similar clinical definitions of central cord syndrome; each was classified as level IV evidence.

document_sections.heading: Patient Demographic Characteristics
document_sections.content: The ≤ 24-hour group contained 188 patients (38.5%), and the > 24-hour group contained 300 patients (61.5%). Male patients accounted for 73.8% and 79.7%, respectively (p = 0.15). Weighted mean age was 52.4 years (95% CI 44.9–61.2 years) in the ≤ 24-hour group and 55.2 years (95% CI 49.3–61.8 years) in the > 24-hour group (p = 0.47). Injury-mechanism data were available for 165 and 236 patients, respectively. Mechanisms did not differ significantly (p = 0.32): falls were most common (49.1% and 60.2%), followed by motor vehicle accidents (32.7% and 28.4%) and sports-related trauma (3.6% and 1.7%). Compression-level data were available for n = 130 and n = 152. C4–5 was the most frequent level (78.5% and 71.1%), followed by C3–4 (13.1% and 16.4%); the groups did not differ significantly (p = 0.35). Neuroimaging data were available for 89 patients in the ≤ 24-hour group and 207 in the > 24-hour group. Cervical stenosis occurred in 73% and 67.1%, disc herniation/fracture/dislocation in 18% and 19.8%, and cord edema in 9% and 13%, respectively. The text reports no significant between-group neuroimaging difference (p > 0.53). At admission, weighted mean ASIA motor score was 63.1% (95% CI 60.8–65.4%) in the ≤ 24-hour group versus 63.8% (95% CI 60.7%–67%) in the > 24-hour group (p = 0.69). TABLE 1 presents the demographic, injury, compression-level, and neuroimaging results.

document_sections.heading: Intervention and Patient Outcomes
document_sections.content: Steroid-use data were available for n = 129 in the ≤ 24-hour group and n = 152 in the > 24-hour group. Steroids were given to 53.5% and 42.8%, respectively (p = 0.72). Surgical-approach data were available for n = 49 and n = 136; approaches were comparable (p = 0.14). Anterior surgery accounted for 44.9% and 37.5%, posterior surgery for 34.7% and 50%, and combined surgery for 20.4% and 12.5%, respectively. Complication data were available for n = 172 and n = 266. The > 24-hour group had a significantly higher surgical complication rate (4.5%) than the ≤ 24-hour group (1.2%, p = 0.05). In the > 24-hour group, the prose reports postoperative hematoma (0.8%), surgical site infection (1.5%), venous thromboembolism (0.8%), and sepsis (1.1%). In the ≤ 24-hour group, surgical site infection (0.6%) and venous thromboembolism (0.6%) were reported; neither postoperative hematoma nor sepsis was recorded. Median clinical follow-up was 12 months (IQR 3–36) in both groups (p > 0.99); included articles used the same fixed final-follow-up duration for both groups. At a mean of 12 months, ASIA motor score improvement was greater in the ≤ 24-hour group, but not significantly so: the between-group mean difference in improvement was 12 (95% CI −20.7 to 44.6, p = 0.33). TABLE 2 presents steroid use, operative approaches, surgical complications, and follow-up, including wound dehiscence among the listed complications.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: In this analysis, surgical timing was not significantly associated with better ASIA motor score outcomes. Surgery ≤ 24 hours was associated with fewer complications, contrary to the commonly held expectation of greater surgical risk with earlier intervention. The authors caution against applying this pattern without regard to the marked variation in ATCCS presentations and advocate an individualized, patient-centered surgical plan.

document_sections.heading: Patient Demographic Characteristics
document_sections.content: Men predominated in both groups: 73.8% in the ≤ 24-hour group and 79.7% in the > 24-hour group, without a significant sex difference (p = 0.15). Weighted mean ages were 52.4 years (95% CI 44.9–61.2) and 55.2 years (95% CI 49.3–61.8), respectively (p = 0.47). The authors considered these demographics consistent with broader spinal cord injury literature. In this discussion, they describe injury-mechanism frequencies as comparable (p = 0.11); the Results section instead reports p = 0.32. Falls led in both groups (49.1% and 60.2%). Rodríguez-Meza et al. reported falls as the principal cause of spinal cord injury in 41.6% of their patients. Motor vehicle accidents ranked second in the present groups (32.7% and 28.4%), followed by sports-related trauma (3.6% and 1.7%). Other research cited by the authors likewise identifies these mechanisms as important contributors; a cited international epidemiological study attributed 25% to 67% of spinal cord injuries to motor vehicle accidents and 5% to 28% to contact sports. Compression most often involved C4–5 (78.5% and 71.1%), then C3–4 (13.1% and 16.4%), without a significant between-group difference (p = 0.35). Cervical stenosis, disc herniation/fracture/dislocation, and cord edema were the leading neuroimaging findings in both groups; the discussion reports no significant difference (p = 0.53). Admission weighted mean ASIA motor scores were also comparable: 63.1% (95% CI 60.8%–65.4%) versus 63.8% (95% CI 60.7%–67%), p = 0.69. The authors interpret this as a similar neurological baseline across surgical-timing groups.

document_sections.heading: Intervention and Patient Outcomes
document_sections.content: Among patients with steroid-use data, 53.5% of the ≤ 24-hour group and 42.8% of the > 24-hour group received steroids, without a significant difference (p = 0.72). The authors note that steroids in acute spinal cord injury remain controversial: some cited studies support possible neuroprotection, whereas others raise concern about complications. Evaluating their value was outside this review's scope. Anterior, posterior, and combined surgical approaches did not differ significantly by timing group (p = 0.14). The authors note that approach selection may depend on injury location and pattern, morphology, ligament status, patient factors, and surgeon preference. Surgical complications were significantly more frequent after > 24 hours (4.5%) than after ≤ 24 hours (1.2%) (p = 0.05). In a separate meta-analysis of traumatic spinal cord injury, Liu et al. reported a significantly higher complication rate with late (≥ 24 hours) surgery (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.91, p = 0.02). A prospective multicenter cohort by Fehlings et al. observed more complications after late (≥ 24 hours) than early (< 24 hours) surgery (30.5% versus 24.2%), although that difference was not statistically significant. The authors state that these findings run counter to the perception that early surgery increases complications. In the present review, the ≤ 24-hour group had surgical site infection and venous thromboembolism, whereas the > 24-hour group had a broader range that included postoperative hematoma, surgical site infection, and sepsis. They suggest a possible safety benefit from earlier surgery but emphasize that proposed explanations—less time with cord compression and secondary injury, or a shorter preoperative stay—are speculative and require study. Surgical decisions should still account for individual patients. Median clinical follow-up was similar: 12 [IQR 3–36] months in the ≤ 24-hour group versus 12 [3–36] months in the > 24-hour group (p > 0.99). This review lacked sufficient data to analyze length of stay. In contrast, Liu et al. associated surgery within 24 hours with a shorter stay (mean day difference −4.76 days, 95% CI −9.19 to −0.32, p = 0.04) and fewer complications (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.91, p = 0.02). At a weighted mean of 12 months after decompression, the present review found greater, but not statistically significant, ASIA motor score improvement after ≤ 24 hours: mean difference in improvement 12 (95% CI −20.7 to 44.6), p = 0.33. Liu et al.'s meta-analysis of traumatic spinal cord injury instead associated early surgery significantly with better neurological outcomes (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.19–2.31, p < 0.01). In Fehlings et al.'s study, patients treated early were 2.8 times more likely to improve by at least 2 grades at 6-month follow-up; after adjustment for preoperative neurological status and steroid use, the OR was 2.83 (95% CI 1.10–7.28, p = 0.03). Another cited study reported improvement of at least 2 grades on the ASIA scale in 27.2% of patients decompressed within 24 hours versus 3% treated later (p = 0.01). Additional cited studies also suggested better neurological outcomes with prompt surgery. The authors attribute their inability to confirm a significant neurological difference to their particular methods and eligibility criteria, which focused on ATCCS and specified timing groups. They view their finding as a more specific perspective rather than a refutation of the wider evidence favoring early treatment. They describe neurological recovery after early surgery as an active research question and, considering complication rates alongside other evidence, advocate early (≤ 24 hours) intervention as a strategy to improve outcomes and limit complications in spinal cord injury.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: The review may be affected by heterogeneity in the published studies and variation in their quality; its accuracy depends on the source studies and their reported data. Every included article provided level IV evidence. Although the complication-rate difference was statistically significant, complications were uncommon. Most articles did not report comorbidities, preventing assessment of whether they delayed surgery; the authors consider it plausible that more comorbidities in the > 24-hour group could have confounded the comparison. Missing or inconsistently reported information may have influenced the analyses. Differences across studies in patient populations, operative techniques, and outcome measures may also reduce comparability.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: The authors' findings challenge the view that early ATCCS surgery causes more complications: the ≤ 24-hour group had a statistically significantly lower complication rate, suggesting a possible safety advantage. Neurological outcomes did not differ significantly between surgery ≤ 24 hours and surgery > 24 hours. They state that surgical decisions should be individualized according to clinical characteristics and injury pattern.
